tagline: OpenRouter-native Agent Zero fork — Temporal, LiteLLM workers, risk scoring, MCP, Rust CLI
description: Khan is a real agent harness built in a concentrated Aug 7–13 sprint: Temporal orchestration, OpenRouter-backed routing, LiteLLM workers, risk scoring, MCP tool surfaces, and a Rust CLI. Ships alongside khanai.app as the public face of the stack. Plugin-first, secret-first operations with a multi-agent coordination board — not a self-hosted GPU or local inference cluster.

showcase.whatItIs: A personal, Linux-backed agent harness with OpenRouter as the default model path. It is a private fork of Agent Zero with Khan's own CLI, secret vault and memory layer on top.
showcase.whoItsFor: One operator running their own agent on their own box, with any model behind it.
showcase.whatLukeBuilt: OpenRouter-native routing through LiteLLM, a host CLI (up, login, ask, chat, memory, sync, remote), a secret vault that keeps keys out of settings files, typed contracts for memory, verification, trust and task runtime, an optional Temporal durable-execution adapter, and the khanai.app landing site and installer.
showcase.status: Built in a concentrated burst in August 2026. The CLI, vault and memory persistence work; the live agent loop is not fully wired to the typed contracts yet, and release downloads are not published.

highlights: Temporal + OpenRouter orchestration with LiteLLM workers
Risk scoring and MCP tool surfaces for agent workflows
architecture: Temporal workflows → OpenRouter/LiteLLM workers → Risk scoring → MCP tools → Rust CLI + khanai.app
finishLine: Shipped Aug 7–13: Temporal + OpenRouter routing, LiteLLM workers, risk scoring, MCP surfaces, Rust CLI, and khanai.app. Remaining polish: harden eval fixtures for production guardrails and expand connector coverage — not a greenfield rebuild.

tagline: Vision-model E2E testing — record once, fingerprint-cache every step, heal on drift, cost-metered per run
description: Argus is an open-source, self-hosted vision-model E2E harness — the open TestDriver alternative. Record a flow once, replay near-free on fingerprint cache, heal only on UI drift, and report results as a check + comment on the GitHub PR. Every vision call is metered from OpenRouter per-call cost into a per-run dollar figure. A grounding specialist model can drive element location verified against the DOM, and an opt-in sandbox lane reproduces code-review findings in a hardened network-less container — a finding that fails on head and passes on base is stamped reproduced.

release.transcript: A launch film for Argus, the vision-model end-to-end testing tool that records once and heals on drift.

highlights: Cache-first replay — zero vision calls on unchanged UI
Cost-explicit — per-run dollar figure on the PR report
Sandbox lane reproduces review findings, stamped not suspected
CodeRabbit-style review surface — formal GitHub reviews that satisfy required-approvals
architecture: Record (Playwright + vision model) → fingerprint cache → replay/heal → GitHub check + formal review with per-call cost ledger
businessContext: Selector-based E2E is brittle and vision E2E is expensive. Argus makes vision testing cost-predictable: cache hits are free, heals are reviewable, and every run carries an exact dollar figure.
scopeAndScale: Published npm package (argus-reviewer-e2e), GitHub Action runner, self-hosted. BYOK via OPENROUTER_API_KEY with hard budget caps.
engineeringDecisions: Fingerprint cache over re-invocation — Vision calls only on drift, not every run
DOM-verified grounding — Model coordinate output checked against the DOM before any click
Cost ledger first-class — Per-call OpenRouter pricing rolled into the run report

tagline: Private automatic work journal for Linux — screenshot sampling, dedupe, vision-model summaries into a readable timeline
description: Dayflow for Omarchy/Wayland is a local-first port of the macOS Dayflow app: a single static Go binary samples a frame every 10 seconds, deduplicates unchanged shots, and every 15 minutes sends the block to a vision model (Gemma 4 via OpenRouter by default) for a plain-language summary. The result is a readable timeline in a QML panel — Today, Standup, Chat, Week, and Settings views — with per-app ignore lists, pause controls, retention pruning, inline edits, and journal chat. Frames and the SQLite store stay in ~/.local/share/dayflow.

release.transcript: A launch film for Dayflow, the private automatic work journal for Linux.

highlights: Local-first — frames and DB never leave ~/.local/share/dayflow
Cheap by design — ~30 frames per block to a $0.09/M-token vision model
~25MB RAM, sub-1% CPU single static binary
Multi-provider routing — vision, summary, standup, and chat can hit different endpoints
Privacy controls — pause toggle, per-app ignore list, automatic frame deletion
architecture: wlroots frame sampler → dedupe → SQLite → 15-min vision summaries (OpenRouter) → QML panel + CLI
engineeringDecisions: Blocks over streams — 15-minute chunks make the timeline readable and the model calls bounded
Edits overlay raw rows — corrections flow into analytics without rewriting history
Dead-letter retries — failed summaries retry 3x then quarantine; `dayflow retry` resets

release.transcript: A launch film for Pace, the production platform for identity, billing and AI for small businesses.

Stripe billing, Stytch auth, a React shell, and Grafana dashboards kept as code.

businessContext: Small businesses need cloud productivity without enterprise complexity. Pace packages identity, billing, and AI into one operator-controlled story on real production infra.
scopeAndScale: Production-stage multi-tenant platform; public surfaces at pacehq.io, app.pacehq.io, observe.pacehq.io, and status.pacehq.io.
engineeringDecisions: Multi-host production — Hetzner compute, Railway app hosting, Cloudflare edge
Grafana-as-code — dashboards and alerts as versioned infrastructure
finishLine: Gateway, auth, and Stripe billing are live (pacehq.io, app.pacehq.io). Remaining ~20%: real tool execution and Python reasoning service hardening — hire is for last-mile finishing.

tagline: Seven public Agent Zero plugins: Argus review, OmaSeal, Jev compaction, device sync, durable runs, GlitchTip, Notion
description: A suite of public plugins for the Agent Zero agent runtime, each in its own repository: pull-request review tools backed by Argus, OmaSeal secret access, Jev context compaction, device sync, durable run state, GlitchTip error reporting, and a Notion ingestion server. They appear here as components of one entry rather than seven.
highlights: Seven plugins, one per capability, each in its own public repository
Argus plugin exposes pull-request review as agent tools
Notion plugin runs as a local stdio MCP server
architecture: Agent Zero runtime → plugin adapters → external service (Argus, Notion, GlitchTip, OmaSeal)

tagline: Pull-request review tools for Agent Zero, backed by Argus
description: Agent Zero plugin adding argus_review and argus_flow tools, backed by Argus, a self-hosted bring-your-own-key pull-request reviewer.
highlights: Exposes review and flow tools to an Agent Zero runtime
architecture: Agent Zero tool call → plugin adapter → Argus reviewer → findings

tagline: One secrets interface for Agent Zero, with masked values only
description: One secrets interface for Agent Zero. Resolves keys through the OmaSeal keyring, 1Password, environment, or an encrypted vault; agents see names and masked values only.
highlights: Single resolution path across four secret backends
Keyring, 1Password, env, and encrypted vault support
architecture: Agent request → secret resolver → backend (keyring/1Password/env/vault) → masked value

tagline: Jev-scored context compaction with tombstone restore
description: Agent Zero plugin for context compaction scored by Jev, with tombstone restore so compacted context can be recovered rather than lost.
highlights: Decision-model scoring drives what gets compacted
architecture: Context window → Jev span scoring → compaction → tombstone store → restore

tagline: Cross-instance settings, chat, and memory sync over Tailscale
description: Cross-instance sync packs for Agent Zero covering settings, chat, and memory, transported over Tailscale and carrying no secrets.
highlights: Settings, chat, and memory kept in sync across instances
Tailscale transport with no secrets in the payload
architecture: Instance state → sync pack → Tailscale transport → peer instance apply

tagline: Restart-survivable agent tasks with a zero-dependency journal
description: Agent Zero plugin making agent tasks durable and restart-survivable: a zero-dependency SQLite journal engine with an optional Restate adapter.
highlights: Optional Restate adapter for stronger guarantees
architecture: Task start → SQLite journal append → restart → journal replay → resume

tagline: Error tracking with request-ID and trace correlation
description: Agent Zero plugin wiring GlitchTip error tracking into agent runs, correlating errors with request IDs and OpenTelemetry traces.
architecture: Agent run → error capture → GlitchTip → request-ID and trace correlation

tagline: Local Notion stdio MCP server with ingestion atoms
description: Notion connector plugin for Agent Zero: a local stdio MCP server plus ingestion atoms for pulling Notion content into an agent's reach.
highlights: Runs as a local stdio MCP server
architecture: Agent Zero → local stdio MCP server → Notion API → ingestion atoms

tagline: iOS-first study app: upload anything, quiz until you know it
description: Upload anything you are studying; Cairn turns it into a study set, quizzes you until you know it, and shows your mastery over time. Built around retrieval practice and successive relearning, with a quality gate on every generated question. Private repository.
highlights: Retrieval practice and successive relearning: quiz until you pass, then again across days
Quality gate on every generated question
One AI gateway through OpenRouter, open-weight models preferred, with Apple on-device models for cheap tasks
iOS built from Linux with xtool, shipped to TestFlight from a Mac
architecture: SwiftUI app → Next.js API on Cloudflare Workers (OpenNext) → D1, R2, Vectorize, Queues → OpenRouter gateway

showcase.whatItIs: A study app. You upload what you are studying, Cairn turns it into a study set, quizzes you until you know it, and shows your mastery over time.
showcase.whoItsFor: One student studying alone; accounts are for ages 13 and up.
showcase.whatLukeBuilt: An iOS-first SwiftUI app built on Linux with xtool, and a Next.js backend on Cloudflare Workers with D1 and R2. One AI gateway through OpenRouter, preferring open-weight models, with Apple on-device Foundation Models for cheap tasks. A quality gate checks every generated question.
showcase.status: Early development. The backend is deployed; an internal TestFlight build is being prepared.

tagline: Command Skyrim NPCs like an RTS, simulated by 0 A.D. over a local WebSocket
description: 0 A.D. runs the simulation headless, a Python host mirrors it over a local WebSocket, and an SKSE plugin renders it as real Skyrim actors from a top-down command camera. Built around the Age of Skyrim mod. Private repository, work in progress.
highlights: Two-process design: headless 0 A.D. plus a Python host, mirrored to the game over WebSocket
SKSE plugin with an RTS camera, box selection, orders and a command grid
Written message protocol between host and plugin
architecture: 0 A.D. (headless) ↔ Python host (RL HTTP) ↔ WebSocket ↔ SKSE plugin → Skyrim NPCs

showcase.whatItIs: A mod that lets you command Skyrim NPCs like an RTS. 0 A.D. owns economy, pathing and combat; Skyrim is the renderer and input device.
showcase.whoItsFor: Skyrim Special Edition players; it is built around the Age of Skyrim mod.
showcase.whatLukeBuilt: The Python bridge host that mirrors the 0 A.D. simulation, the SKSE plugin that renders it as Skyrim actors with a top-down camera, selection, orders and a command grid, and the WebSocket protocol between them.
showcase.status: Work in progress, Windows only. The host is covered by offline tests; the plugin UI has not had a long human playtest.

tagline: No-account iPhone remote for an electric scooter, over Bluetooth LE
description: A lightweight Swift/SwiftUI app that talks to a HopCycle W3 Max electric scooter directly over Bluetooth LE: a native port of the Voltix FF60 protocol recovered from the vendor's Android app. No backend, no cloud, no account. Private repository.
highlights: BLE protocol recovered from the vendor's Android app: service UUIDs, frame layout, CRC-16
Live dashboard (speed, battery, fault code), lock, lights, gear, speed limit, cruise control
Unbind, reset and OTA commands deliberately not implemented
No backend, no cloud, no account binding
architecture: SwiftUI → CoreBluetooth → scooter BLE service FF60 (notify and write characteristics)

showcase.whatItIs: An iPhone remote for a HopCycle W3 Max electric scooter that talks to it directly over Bluetooth LE, with no backend, cloud or account.
showcase.whoItsFor: Owners of a HopCycle W3 Max who want control without binding to the vendor's cloud account.
showcase.whatLukeBuilt: A native Swift/SwiftUI port of the Voltix FF60 BLE protocol, decoded from the vendor's Android app: scan and connect, a live dashboard, lock and unlock, lights, gear, speed limit and cruise control. Unbind, reset and OTA commands are deliberately left out so the app cannot brick the scooter.
showcase.status: Working client. UUIDs, frame layout and CRC are high confidence; telemetry decoding is provisional until checked against the scooter's display.

tagline: This site: a star-chart portfolio with live GitHub activity and a dossier per project
description: The Next.js app behind luke-the-duke.com. The homepage is a solar map with a primary orbit of featured systems and a secondary orbit of the rest of the catalog; each project has a dossier page. A GitHub App ingests about 90 days of activity, rendered as condensed charts and grouped pull requests. The catalog in src/data is the single source of truth, nothing is auto-discovered.
highlights: Solar-map homepage: primary and secondary orbits driven from catalog data
About 90 days of GitHub App activity, shown as charts and grouped PRs with a 7d / 30d / 90d toggle
Dossier page per project, with private work shown through scrubbed labels only
Catalog SOP and tests keep the single source of truth consistent
architecture: Catalog (src/data) → GitHub App ingest (ISR) → activity aggregation → orbit and dossier pages

tagline: Context compaction for agent harnesses: keep what still matters, tombstone the rest
description: A retention filter for agent transcripts, not a summarizer. A decision model scores each span against the conversation's moving highlight; top spans stay verbatim, the middle band becomes one-line tombstones, and the full transcript stays on disk. An MCP restore server rehydrates any tombstone on demand. A heuristic scorer works offline with no keys.
highlights: Scores spans on relevance to the current topic and how load-bearing they are
Token-budget knapsack: keep verbatim, tombstone, or drop
context-restore MCP server rehydrates tombstoned spans
Stdlib-only Python; Claude Code adapter ready, Codex and OpenCode next
architecture: Transcript → spans → highlight → score → budget knapsack → kept spans + tombstones → MCP restore

tagline: Browser-to-sandbox pipeline that turns live SaaS pricing pages into CSV and JSON
description: A Solari demo built for a SWE intern application. One cloud browser loads each configured pricing page, a headless sandbox parses it with a shared parser in two modes (class-based for React pricing cards, heading-based heuristic for conventional pages), and the host merges the per-site output into one CSV and one JSON. The parser is unit-tested against sample HTML without an API key.
highlights: Multi-URL pipeline from cloud browser to isolated sandbox
Two parsing modes for different pricing-page layouts
Combined pricing.csv and pricing.json from a verified live run
Runs inside the Solari Free plan: one browser, one sandbox, released on exit
architecture: sites.json → cloud browser → HTML upload → sandbox parser → per-site output → merged CSV and JSON
